title: Agent Memory: Accuracy, Cost, and Gaps.
excerpt: With 1M-token context windows, agent memory no longer wins by beating full context on short histories. Its clear value today is cost; persistence and learning remain open problems.
tldr: Long context weakens the old accuracy pitch for memory: when the history fits in the prompt, full context often matches or beats retrieval-style memory.
The part that clearly works today is cost and latency. Memory trades write-time work for cheaper repeated reads at roughly fixed accuracy.
The hard promises are still open: updating stale facts, handling contradictions, forgetting safely, learning reusable procedures, and testing memory beyond the effective context window.

title: Agent Reliability Is a Systems Problem: Checking Claims Against the Work Record
excerpt: A follow-up on agent-system reliability: why checking whether an agent's claims are supported by its own trace, files, and git state is different from checking whether the work is correct.
tldr: Agent reports fail in ordinary sentences: tests pass, a citation was read, a CSV has certain rows, or an output came from files the session never touched.
`provcheck-claude` checks support, not correctness: it compares the agent's claims against the transcript, files, git state, and captured diffs.
The useful reliability surface is systems-level. Code should verify hard evidence, the model should handle extraction and ambiguous judgment, and the report should say what was checked.

title: Black-box Characterization of LLM Serving Caches: Contracts, Asymmetries, and Prompt Design
excerpt: A black-box measurement of DeepSeek, OpenAI, and Anthropic prompt caches: why prefix identity matters, where provider contracts differ, and how prompt layout becomes a systems interface.
tldr: Prompt caches are prefix contracts. Stable material must appear before variable material; repeated text in the middle or at the end does not buy reuse.
DeepSeek, OpenAI, and Anthropic agree on prefix identity but differ in visible token units, cache horizon, branchability, and whether cache breakpoints are explicit.

For applications, layout is a systems interface: put documents, repo context, schemas, and rubrics before the question; keep file order canonical; append volatile material late; log cache-hit counters.

title: Will AI bankrupt my lab?
excerpt: A shared API key, a negative balance, and a harder question for research labs: if frontier-model access becomes part of the cost of doing research, who pays for the tokens?
tldr: A shared lab API key turned routine coding-agent use into a real research bill: more than $3,000 in April, with two students spending over $2,000 in about a week.
Token access is becoming research infrastructure, closer to GPU time or cluster allocation than a casual software subscription.
Labs need explicit norms: separate keys, budgets before usage, alerts and hard limits, cheaper models for routine work, and protection against pushing research costs onto students.

title: Auto Research Is Real. It's Just Not What People Think.
excerpt: Auto research is real and getting better fast. But it's not replacing researchers — it's changing where human effort matters. After months of building these systems, here's what I've learned about verification, deskilling, and taste.
tldr: Auto-research agents can move through the workflow, but they are still execution-fragile: polished papers, plots, and summaries can hide broken environments or experiments that never really ran.
The bottleneck is verification. Code has compilers and tests; research has sparse, delayed feedback, so errors can survive across literature review, implementation, experiments, and writing.
AI compresses the middle of research. Humans still own the ends: choosing worthwhile problems, judging evidence, spotting failure, and training taste.

title: Introducing Research Copilot — An AI Lab Partner for Academics
excerpt: Research Copilot is an open-source AI desktop app built for PhD students, postdocs, and faculty — it searches literature across four databases, writes papers with verified citations, runs data analysis, and helps draft grant proposals, all in one place.
tldr: Research Copilot is an open-source desktop research assistant meant to help you think through ideas, not just generate text.
It searches Semantic Scholar, arXiv, OpenAlex, and DBLP, deduplicates results, and verifies citations against real search results.
The app lives in your project folder, can run workspace tools, keeps papers and notes across sessions, and can be extended with project-specific Markdown skills.

title: Introducing RAM Desktop — A Research Assistant That Works With You
excerpt: RAM Desktop is a macOS research assistant that breaks your question into tasks, collects evidence, and advances the work round by round — pausing at key checkpoints for your review.
tldr: RAM Desktop is a macOS research assistant that decomposes a research question into tasks, gathers evidence, and advances the run in reviewable rounds.
The interface is built for human-in-the-loop research: Dashboard, Taskboard, Console, Review Inbox, Evidence, and Audit views keep progress and provenance visible.
It works best on bounded, measurable questions. Because it can write and run code inside the project workspace, use a clean folder and watch the Console for sensitive or first-time runs.

title: University Isn't a Job Factory — and Computer Science Isn't Ending
excerpt: Two recurring fears: universities should be industry pipelines, and AI is ending software jobs. I think both framings are wrong — and the reasons why matter.
tldr: A university is not a company's training pipeline. Its deeper job is to build judgment, discipline, confidence, and a foundation students can carry beyond any one stack.
AI does not make universities obsolete; it makes fundamentals and AI fluency both more important.
Computer science is not ending. Its center of gravity is shifting toward the systems, security, data, evaluation, governance, and integration work that turns AI from demos into infrastructure.

title: Hello World — Reviving My Personal Site
excerpt: After years of redirecting to Google Sites, I finally rebuilt my homepage from scratch. Here's why and what's next.
tldr: I rebuilt `daidong.github.io` as a personal academic site instead of redirecting to a Google Sites profile.
The site is intentionally small: plain HTML and CSS, no framework, no build step, a light/dark theme, and a client-side Markdown blog.
The blog will be a place for research directions, mentoring notes, and academic productivity workflows.
